Promotional codes — design

Date: 2026-08-30 Status: approved (design), not yet implemented

Problem

There is no way to sell the manual at anything other than Purchase::PRICE_CENTS. Running a campaign today means either changing the constant for everyone or recording sales by hand through /antesis-admin/enrollments.

We want a promotional code: a buyer types a string at /pagar, the total drops by a fixed amount, and the sale is recorded with the code that produced it.

Scope

In scope:

  • One discount kind: a fixed amount off, in centavos. No percentages.
  • An expiry datetime and an active/inactive flag.
  • Unlimited uses, globally and per buyer. A second purchase by the same email with the same code is a legitimate second sale, exactly as a repeat Stripe purchase already is.
  • All three payment paths: Stripe Payment Element, PayPal, and the SPEI bank transfer.
  • An admin screen to create codes, edit live ones, and see who redeemed each.

Out of scope (YAGNI):

  • Percentage discounts, per-code usage caps, per-email limits, product scoping, stacking two codes, free (100%-off) purchases, and attaching a code to an admin enrollment at /antesis-admin/enrollments.

Decisions

| Question | Decision | |—|—| | Discount kind | Fixed centavos off | | Payment methods | Stripe, PayPal, and bank transfer | | Expired / inactive code at payment time | Never honored. Every money endpoint re-validates on every call. | | Where the redemption is recorded | Columns on purchases, no join table | | Floor | Charge clamps at MINIMUM_CHARGE_CENTS (1000 = $10 MXN) | | Expiry | Required datetime | | Matching | Case-insensitive, admin-authored string | | Uses | Unlimited, no per-email check | | Admin UI | Own Inertia page under /antesis-admin, linked from /a | | Editing a code | All fields while it has zero redemptions; once redeemed, only active |

Approach

A server-side price resolver, plus attribution carried in the processor object.

The client may send a code string. It may never send an amount. Every endpoint that spends money resolves the price itself through one object, re-validating active and expires_at on each call — so a code that expires between the buyer applying it and paying is simply not applied, and a hand-crafted POST quoting a dead code gets full price.

Attribution has to survive into the webhook, which carries no request params and can be the path that records the purchase. So the resolved code id rides in the processor object the same way terms acceptance and the product tag already do: Stripe metadata.promo_code_id, PayPal custom_id.

Two alternatives were rejected:

  • Session-carried code. Storing the validated code in the Rails session adds a second source of truth the webhook cannot read, and since expired codes are never honored, per-call re-validation is required regardless.
  • Pending-redemption row keyed by the idempotency key. PayPal’s capture id differs from the order id, so the key does not survive to the webhook. custom_id does.

Data model

promo_codes (new)

| Column | Type | Notes | |—|—|—| | code | string, not null | As typed by the admin. Unique index on LOWER(code) — the users.nickname pattern. | | discount_cents | bigint, not null | Validated > 0. | | expires_at | datetime, not null | | | active | boolean, not null, default true | |

Model:

class PromoCode < ApplicationRecord
  MINIMUM_CHARGE_CENTS = 1_000 # $10 MXN — Stripe's MXN floor.

  has_many :purchases

  validates :code, presence: true, uniqueness: { case_sensitive: false }
  validates :discount_cents, numericality: { only_integer: true, greater_than: 0 }
  validates :expires_at, presence: true

  # Lookup is case-insensitive, hitting the LOWER(code) index.
  def self.find_by_code(raw)
    where("LOWER(code) = ?", raw.to_s.strip.downcase).first
  end

  def redeemable? = active? && expires_at.future?
  def redeemed? = purchases.exists?
end

As with users.nickname, the index is the authority and the validation only proposes: any insert path must be ready for both RecordNotUnique and a RecordInvalid with code: :taken, which mean the same thing.

purchases (altered)

| Column | Type | Notes | |—|—|—| | promo_code_id | bigint, nullable, FK, indexed | Nil for a full-price sale. | | discount_cents | bigint, not null, default 0 | What this sale was discounted by. |

amount_cents keeps its existing meaning — what was actually charged — and stays sourced from the Stripe/PayPal object, never from a constant. The two new columns only annotate it. Consequently, editing a promo_codes row never rewrites what a past sale recorded, which is the same non-overwrite guarantee amount_cents was introduced for (see db/migrate/20260825120000_add_amount_to_purchases.rb).

Migration backfills nothing: promo_code_id is nil and discount_cents is 0 for every existing row, which is already true of them.

bank_transfer_payment_intents (altered)

| Column | Type | Notes | |—|—|—| | amount_cents | bigint, not null | Backfilled with the literal 69000, not PRICE_CENTS. | | promo_code_id | bigint, nullable, FK, indexed | |

The reference is a ledger of what we told a buyer to deposit, so the amount we quoted has to be on the row: otherwise a deposit for an unexpected sum cannot be explained from the database. Same backfill-with-a-literal rule as the purchases.amount_cents migration — the constant may change later; history may not.

Pricing

One object is the authority for what a checkout costs:

# app/concepts/checkout/price.rb (or app/services/checkout_price.rb)
Checkout::Price.resolve(code_string) # => Checkout::Price
#   #amount_cents    what to charge, clamped at PromoCode::MINIMUM_CHARGE_CENTS
#   #discount_cents  PRICE_CENTS - amount_cents (the *effective* discount)
#   #promo_code      the PromoCode, or nil
#   #label           "$490 MXN"

Rules:

  • A blank, unknown, inactive or expired code resolves to full price with promo_code: nil. It is not an error at the payment endpoints — the buyer just pays full price, and the apply endpoint (below) is where a bad code produces a visible message.
  • amount_cents = [PRICE_CENTS - discount_cents, MINIMUM_CHARGE_CENTS].max. A code worth more than the manual charges $10 rather than going negative.
  • discount_cents is recomputed from the clamped amount, so a clamped sale records the discount it actually received, not the code’s nominal value.

Purchase.price_label gains an optional argument (def self.price_label(cents = PRICE_CENTS)) and keeps deriving the string from cents, so the shown and charged amounts still cannot drift.

Checkout endpoints

POST /pagar/promocion — apply

CheckoutsController#apply_promo_code. CSRF-protected like its neighbours, and rate-limited under its own name: ("promo-code", 10/min) — a shared name: would let one endpoint eat another’s budget, which is why the existing limits are already named.

Request: { code }. No email, no terms — this reveals nothing and spends nothing.

Response, on a redeemable code:

{ "code": "LANZAMIENTO", "discountLabel": "-$200 MXN",
  "priceLabel": "$490 MXN", "amountCents": 49000 }

Otherwise 422 with { "error": "invalid" }; the page renders one Spanish message (“Ese código no es válido o ya expiró”) for unknown, inactive and expired alike — distinguishing them would tell a stranger which codes exist.

amountCents is returned solely so the client can update the Stripe Elements options (see below). It is display data; the charge is still computed server-side on every payment call.

The three payment endpoints

Each takes an optional promo_code param, resolves it, and uses the resolved amount:

  • CheckoutsController#create_intent — creates the PaymentIntent at price.amount_cents and adds promo_code_id to the metadata beside the existing product and terms_accepted_at.
  • Paypal::CheckoutsController#create_order — creates the order at price.amount_cents and passes the code id into custom_id.
  • CheckoutsController#create_bank_transfer — passes amount_cents:/promo_code: into BankTransferPaymentIntent.for, which now updates those two columns on an existing row when they differ. The reference itself never changes; one email keeps one reference forever, which is the invariant that makes a deposit reconcilable. #email_bank_transfer and BankTransferMailer#instructions read intent.amount_cents instead of Purchase.price_label, so the mail always quotes what the modal quoted.

custom_id format

Today: "#{MANUAL_PRODUCT}|#{email}", parsed with split("|", 2). New: "#{MANUAL_PRODUCT}|#{email}|#{promo_code_id}", third part optional.

Purchase.paypal_custom_parts changes to split("|", 3) and must keep accepting a two-part value — orders created before this ships are still in flight when it deploys. PayPal caps custom_id at 127 characters; product tag plus a long email plus an integer id stays well inside it, but the builder should drop the promo part rather than truncate if the whole ever exceeds it.

Recording the purchase

Purchase::PaymentSource gains two members, promo_code_id and discount_cents, filled by each constructor:

  • .from_payment_intent — reads intent.metadata["promo_code_id"], and derives discount_cents as PRICE_CENTS - intent.amount floored at 0. Deriving it from the intent’s own amount (rather than re-reading the code) keeps the rule that a sale records what it actually charged.
  • .from_paypal_capture — the same, from the third custom_id part and the capture’s own amount.
  • .cash — always nil / 0. Attaching a code to an admin enrollment is out of scope; the admin types the amount they were actually paid.

Purchase::Operation::Record#record_purchase writes both new fields only inside the create_or_find_by! block, exactly like amount_cents — a re-delivered webhook or a second browser return must find the existing row and leave its recorded discount untouched.

An unknown or since-deleted promo_code_id in metadata must not fail the purchase: the write is promo_code_id: id if PromoCode.exists?(id), or the FK is left nil. A paid sale never fails over an annotation.

Checkout page (Checkout.jsx)

Below the PayPal button: a text link “agregar código promocional” that reveals a text input and an “aplicar” button (a button, not a nested form — the page already has one form and handleSubmit pays). On success:

  • The summary aside shows the original price struck through above the new total, and the pay button reads Pagar $490 MXN.
  • A small “código LANZAMIENTO aplicado” line with a way to remove it.

Three implementation hazards, all of them the kind that pass a stubbed test and fail in a real browser:

  1. <Elements> mounts in deferred-intent mode with a fixed amount. Applying a code must change that option, or Stripe raises at confirm time on the amount mismatch. This means the applied-promo state must live in the top-level Checkout component (which renders <Elements>), not inside CheckoutForm — react-stripe-js forwards an options.amount change to elements.update(), so passing the new amount down is enough.
  2. The PayPal button’s callbacks are zoid-hosted and capture stale closures. Checkout.jsx already routes email and “can pay” through emailRef/canPayRef for this reason; the applied code needs a promoCodeRef on the same pattern, or createOrder will post the code as it stood when the button rendered.
  3. parsePrice parses the display label only to feed Elements’ payment-method picker. With a discount the top-level component now has amountCents directly from the apply response; prefer it when present and keep parsePrice(priceLabel) as the no-code path.

Everything else in the file’s existing conventions holds: default-theme tokens only, no browser globals outside effects/handlers (this page renders through SSR), straight corners, hairlines.

The bank transfer modal needs no structural change — it already renders details.amountLabel, which the server now computes from the intent’s stored amount.

Admin

Route, inside the existing admin authenticate block and before the RailsAdmin mount (which owns the whole /antesis-admin prefix):

get   "/antesis-admin/promo-codes",     to: "admin/promo_codes#index"
post  "/antesis-admin/promo-codes",     to: "admin/promo_codes#create"
patch "/antesis-admin/promo-codes/:id", to: "admin/promo_codes#update"

Admin::PromoCodesController renders one Inertia page, Admin/PromoCodes, following Admin::EnrollmentsController’s shape: a private render_page that re-renders the same component with an error: or a success marker, rather than redirect-and-flash.

Props: each code with code, discountLabel, expiresAt, active, redemptionCount, editable (= redemptionCount.zero?), and its redemptions (buyer email, nickname, date, discountLabel, amountLabel) — one query with includes(:purchases), not one per row.

The page shows a create form, then a list of codes with state, expiry and redemption count, each expandable to its redemptions.

Editing rule. While a code has zero redemptions, every field is editable. Once it has been redeemed, only active may change — deactivating a live campaign has to stay possible, but silently renaming or re-pricing a code that buyers are holding must not. The controller enforces this server-side (it filters the permitted params by redeemed?); the page merely reflects it, since a disabled input is not a security boundary.

A link is added to Admin::HubController’s links array: “Códigos promocionales” / “Crea y edita promociones, y mira quién las usó”.

Testing

RSpec (spec/):

  • PromoCode — case-insensitive lookup and uniqueness; redeemable? across active/inactive × future/past expiry.
  • Checkout::Price — full price for blank/unknown/inactive/expired; discounted price for a live code; the clamp, including that discount_cents reports the clamped (effective) discount, not the nominal one.
  • POST /pagar/promocion — success shape; one identical 422 for unknown, inactive and expired; rate limit.
  • create_intent — the intent is created at the discounted amount and carries promo_code_id in metadata; an expired code produces a full-price intent with no metadata code.
  • PayPal — create_order uses the discounted amount; custom_id round-trips three parts, and a legacy two-part value still parses.
  • Stripe webhook — a purchase recorded from a webhook alone (no browser return) lands with the right promo_code_id and discount_cents.
  • Purchase::Operation::Record — a second arrival for the same idempotency key leaves discount_cents and promo_code_id untouched; an unknown promo_code_id records the purchase with a nil code rather than failing.
  • Bank transfer — .for updates the amount on an existing reference without changing the reference number; the mailer quotes the stored amount.
  • Admin — non-admin is refused; create/edit; a redeemed code rejects every field but active even when the params are posted directly.

No new Vitest coverage: the promo logic added to Checkout.jsx is React state and fetch, not the pure-function kind that lib/highlights/ extracts. The Elements amount update and the PayPal ref are verified by driving the real page in a browser, which is the only thing that catches this class of bug (the elements.submit() ordering has the same property).

Risks

  • The Elements amount mismatch (hazard 1) is silent under every stub and loud only against a live Payment Element. Verify in a browser before shipping.
  • In-flight PayPal orders created before deploy carry a two-part custom_id. The parser must stay tolerant.
  • A code edited mid-campaign changes future sales only. That is intended and is what the redeemed? lock plus per-purchase discount_cents guarantee.
